answer.exemplar: The two checks answer different questions, and the confusion that produces every bad version of this design comes from noticing that they usually test the same thing. The boundary check asks whether this request is a request the service is willing to interpret at all: is the document well formed, is the field the right type, is it within the size the transport will carry. Its whole purpose is to fail cheaply and early, before the value has been copied into anything the rest of the service treats as real, and before the service has spent a connection, a transaction or a round trip to find out. That is why it belongs where the value arrives, and why it is the check that has to be exhaustive, because it is the only place that sees every value. The domain check asks whether the thing the value describes is in a state that permits this operation: a suspended customer, a closed account, an order already shipped. Its purpose is not to inspect input at all but to keep the model itself honest, so that the rule holds for every caller rather than for the callers that remembered to check. That is also why it cannot be replaced by the boundary check, because a value that entered legitimately through one route will be produced by other routes that never pass the handler: a queue consumer replaying yesterday's events, a scheduled reconciliation, an administrative repair, a migration. The wrong version of this design puts the shape rules in the domain, where they are checked on every path and reject nobody before any work is done, and the other wrong version puts the invariants in the handler, where they hold for one route only. The practical consequence for review is that the two belong in different files and are tested by different means: the boundary by sending it bad requests at the edge, the domain by driving the same operation through the second and third routes and watching it still refuse.

A script block is delimited by the end of the block itself rather than by quotes, so what matters there is a different set of characters again, and a value placed in a script is read by a parser that has nothing to do with markup. Everything outside that set is a request another origin's page could cause the service to do something it would not otherwise do, and here the exposure is on the service's side, so the browser asks the service first. A useful standing test for a policy is to ask what would happen if a request arrived from an origin nobody had ever heard of, because that is precisely the case reflection allows and precisely the case a fixed list refuses.

answer.exemplar: The reason a log is not merely a record is that it is an input to something. Alerting rules read it, a responder searches it at three in the morning, a later auditor trusts it, and in most systems a parser turns each line into fields before any of that happens. A value that can end a line can therefore choose what the next line says, and every one of those readers is downstream of a decision the person who supplied the value has just made. Demonstrated on a throwaway file: a name followed by a newline and a plausible record produced two records when the file was read line by line, and the second carried its own timestamp and its own source address, so it was not a corrupted record but an indistinguishable one. That word is what makes this a security problem rather than a tidiness problem, because every downstream reader has no way to tell the two apart and will act on the forged one exactly as it would act on the real one. Two consequences follow that are worth stating separately, since they are what a reviewer is actually arguing about. The first is operational: a responder who cannot trust the log cannot use it to decide what to preserve, and an investigator who cannot trust it cannot use it to establish what happened, so a single writable field damages the evidential value of the whole file rather than of one line. The second is that the log is then a place an attacker can write, which converts a read-only information leak into a channel, and the cheapest route to that outcome is a field that is convenient to log and never quoted. The repair is inexpensive and it belongs where the value is turned into text rather than in the logging configuration, because a configuration-level filter is a list somebody has to remember to extend, while a structured logger asks the value to describe itself and therefore cannot be defeated by adding a character. Serialising the value was confirmed the same way: the break becomes two characters inside one field, so the file still holds exactly one record. Two habits are worth naming next to it. The logger should carry an identifier that it chose rather than one derived from the request, so a forged line cannot borrow a real correlation value and appear to belong to a request that happened. And the retention of a security log should be longer than the period in which the party who wrote the value expects to be noticed, because the person best placed to explain a strange record is the one who wrote it, and that interest is short-lived.
